Inner Monologue is a new training and inference setup for audio language models that predicts time‑aligned text tokens before audio tokens, using text tokens as a per‑timestep prefix to the semantic token [MOSHI:1:c007]. It significantly improves the factuality and linguistic quality of generated speech [MOSHI:1:c007] and almost triples Moshi’s accuracy on spoken question‑answering benchmarks, markedly raising performance over prior work while only marginally increasing inference cost [MOSHI:5.5:c091].

The routing module measures the similarity between adjacent encoder outputs by computing cosine similarity of learned query and key projections for each position, forming a boundary probability p_t = ½ (1 − (q_t^⊤ k_{t‑1})/(‖q_t‖‖k_{t‑1}‖)) that lies in [0, 1] [HNET:2.2.1:c023]. A hard boundary indicator b_t is then set to 1 when p_t ≥ 0.5 and 0 otherwise, with p_1 defined as 1.0 to start the sequence with a boundary [HNET:2.2.1:c023]. The module therefore places chunk boundaries at positions where the cosine similarity between consecutive representations drops enough to make p_t ≥ 0.5, reflecting a contextual or semantic shift [HNET:2.2.1:c023].

The routing module computes cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs by projecting each output \hat{x}_t to a query q_t = W_q \hat{x}_t and a key k_t = W_k \hat{x}_t, then forms a boundary probability p_t = ½ (1 − (q_t^⊤ k_{t‑1})/(‖q_t‖‖k_{t‑1}‖)) which lies in [0, 1] [HNET:2.2.1:c023]. It then creates a hard boundary indicator b_t by setting b_t = 1 if p_t ≥ 0.5 and 0 otherwise, with p_1 defined as 1.0 to start the sequence with a boundary [HNET:2.2.1:c023].

The authors chose sinusoidal positional encodings because they hypothesized that the sinusoid function would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PE_{pos+k} can be represented as a linear function of PE_{pos}, and because it may enable extrapolation to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training [AIAYN:3.5:c020]. They also experimented with learned positional embeddings and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results, with the learned version yielding a dev perplexity of 4.92 and BLEU of 25.7, essentially the same as the base model [AIAYN:3.5:c020][AIAYN:T3:r08][AIAYN:6.2:c031].

Moshi’s theoretical latency of 160 ms is achieved by the model’s streaming, hierarchical architecture that is pretrained with an acoustic delay of 2 and finetuned with an acoustic delay of 1, which together set the target delay for real‑time operation[MOSHI:5.3:c083]. This design choice is highlighted in the introduction as giving Moshi a theoretical latency of 160 ms, which is lower than the 230 ms average measured in natural conversations across ten languages[MOSHI:1:c005]. In practice, Moshi runs with a latency of about 200 ms, as reported in the abstract[MOSHI:abstract:c002]. This practical latency is still below the typical natural‑conversation response time of a few hundred milliseconds and specifically lower than the 230 ms average observed in real human dialogue[MOSHI:1:c005].

H‑Net builds its hierarchy by applying a dynamic‑chunking layer that uses a routing module to draw content‑dependent chunk boundaries and a downsampler that keeps vectors at those boundary positions, thereby creating a compressed representation that can be further processed in subsequent stages [HNET:1:c012][HNET:T6:r03]. The architecture can be iterated, so that the output of one dynamic‑chunking stage becomes the input to a second, yielding a nested, multi‑stage hierarchy [HNET:3.1:c049]. Empirically, adding the second stage improves performance: H‑Net (2‑stage) is significantly better than H‑Net (1‑stage) [HNET:3.1:c049].

H‑Net’s hierarchy is created by a dynamic‑chunking layer that includes a routing module for drawing chunk boundaries and a downsampler that retains vectors at those boundary indicators, reducing sequence length while preserving semantically important positions [HNET:1:c012]. The model can apply this dynamic chunking iteratively, forming two nested stages (S=2) as shown in the architectural overview [HNET:1:c012]. H‑Net (2‑stage) is significantly better than H‑Net (1‑stage), demonstrating that adding a second dynamic‑chunking stage improves performance [HNET:3.1:c049].
